newsitem.title: BURUNDI: Burundi army says sanctions hit the weakest first.
newsitem.headline: Burundi army says sanctions hit the weakest first.

text.p: Burundi authorities said on Monday sanctions imposed by neighbouring countries hurt the weak and if they were not lifted soon the country would explode.
Lieutenant-Colonel Longin Minani, spokesman for the army which seized power in Burundi on July 25, said an embargo on the country since July 31 was hitting those who could least afford it.
"For us the sanctions have been put there unfairly," he told Reuters. "Measures...should be for the good of the population."

"We do not have fertilisers. Next year what will happen?" said Minani, arguing Buyoya's government had met the demands of regional states behind sanctions by lifting bans on political parties and parliament.
The sanctions imposed after Buyoya's take over of power have cut off oil imports to the landlocked country and blocked exports of coffee, its main hard currency earner.
But regional leaders who imposed sanctions on July 31 also demand talks without conditions between all parties to Burundi's conflict. Buyoya says the rebels have to lay down their weapons first.
Minani said rebels were being helped by neighbouring states and were continuing their activities unabated despite sanctions.

In an interview published in Kenya's East African weekly on Wednesday, Tutsi military ruler Pierre Buyoya said: "If this country remains under sanctions for two or three (more) months, all is going to explode."
"I say that the embargo and sanctions are destroying the peace process right now," said the retired army major, adding he was ready to negotiate a lifting of the sanctions.

Meanwhile, officials from a faction of the main Hutu party, split since the army coup, said earlier on Monday they backed exiled party president Jean Minani and were committed to solving Burundi's conflict peacefully.
The group made the announcement in a statement a week after another wing of the Frodebu party elected rebel leader Leonard Nyangoma as its president and endorsed armed struggle.

Frodebu Secretary-General Augustin Nzojibwami said party leaders at the weekend in Bujumbura confirmed their commitment to a peaceful resolution to Burundi's conflict between Hutu rebels and the Tutsi-dominated military and supported Minani.
"Participants reaffirmed that there is no military solution to the Burundian conflict. Only negotiations...will bring peace to Burundi," the party said in a statement after the talks.
Frodebu has been divided since the army took over and Buyoya succeeded President Sylvestre Ntibantunganya, a Frodebu member.

Nzojibwami told Reuters on Wednesday several Frodebu leaders who took refuge in the German embassy in Bujumbura after the coup left their sanctuary at the weekend after Buyoya lifted the ban on political parties.
The statement made no direct mention of the split within the party but former foreign minister Venerand Bakevyumusaya, who lost his post in the coup, told Reuters Minani was still the leader.
More than 150,000 people -- mostly civilians -- have died in three years of violence between the army and rebels from the Hutu majority, which makes up 85 percent of the country's six million people.
